text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

I can draft this. A few answers will make the letter stronger and more specific. Answer whichever you can. If you don't know one, I'll leave it out rather than guess.

1. **Does the college ask referees anything specific?** For example a form, a list of prompts, or a named contact to address it to. If so, please paste it in. Also, what name, farm name, location and contact details should go in the signature?

2. **How did he catch those 9 mastitis cases?** Was it software alerts like conductivity or somatic cell counts, changes in milk yield, or noticing the cows' behavior at milking? And do you know what catching them early saved, such as cows kept in the herd, less milk dumped, or lower treatment costs? Even a rough figure helps.

3. **Should the letter mention the 5-week leave last summer?** The college won't know about it unless you tell them. I'd suggest leaving it out, since it was a family emergency and his record otherwise is 2 missed shifts in 3 years. If you want it in, I'd describe it briefly and fairly.

4. **Should the letter mention his written English?** I'd suggest bringing it up only to say he's taking a night class on his own initiative. That shows he spots his own gaps and works on them. Or would you rather leave it out completely?

5. **Would you hire him back after the program, or give him more responsibility?** Something like "I would hire him back as herd manager tomorrow" is often the strongest line in a reference letter. Do you know what he wants to do once he finishes?

1. I don't know of a form or specific prompts. It goes in through the college's online portal and it's due February 1. I don't have a contact name. Sign it Mike Hollis, Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy. My number is 555-0187, and they can call me.

2. I don't know exactly how he spotted them. The vet told us catching them early saved us about $8,000.

3. Go with your suggestion and leave it out.

4. Go with your suggestion and just mention the night class.

5. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program. I don't know about after, and I don't know what he wants to do once he finishes.

<final_document>
Dear Admissions Committee,

I am writing to recommend Tomás for your two-year Agricultural Technology program. I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow operation. Tomás has worked for me for three years, since he was 19. I would put him up against anyone I have employed.

For the past three years Tomás has run our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. No one checks on him at that hour. He is responsible for the herd, the equipment and the milk from start to finish, and the work gets done right. In three years he has missed two shifts. I don't hand that shift to just anyone, and I have never had reason to regret giving it to him.

Tomás also took on more than his job required. He learned our herd management software and now uses it to flag sick cows for our veterinarian. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early. Our vet estimates that this saved the farm about $8,000. Nobody asked him to do that. He saw how the data connected to the animals in front of him and made it part of his routine. That is the reason I think he belongs in your program. He already thinks like a technician, and formal training will give him the depth to go further.

He also recognizes his own weak spots and works on them. His spoken English is strong. On his own initiative he is taking a night class to bring his written English up to the same level. He did not wait for anyone to tell him to.

I want to see Tomás succeed in this program. While he is enrolled, I will keep a part-time weekend position open for him at Hollis Dairy.

I recommend him without reservation. If you would like to talk about him further, please call me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
555-0187
</final_document>

The letter fits on one page as written. Before it goes into the portal by February 1, a few things to check:

- **Date:** I didn't put a date on it. Portal submissions are dated automatically, but add one if you'd like.
- **His last name:** I only used "Tomás." Add his full name, especially in the first sentence, so the letter gets matched to his application.
- **The vet's figure:** I described the $8,000 as your vet's estimate. That's accurate, and it's more convincing coming from the vet than from you.
- **Left out on purpose:** As agreed, the letter doesn't mention the 5-week leave. It mentions his English only through the night class. It also says nothing about how he spotted the mastitis cases or what he plans to do after the program, because you didn't know those things.
